title: Infra: GPU fleet capacity, cloud accounts & networking, Terraform/IaC modules, CI/CD runbook
author: Priya Nambiar
body:
Summary

This team wiki consolidates operational guidance for the GPU fleet and capacity, cloud accounts and networking, Terraform/IaC module usage, and CI/CD build and deploy patterns. It is intended for infra engineers, platform engineers, on-call SREs, and engineers onboarding to GPU-related workstreams. Use this doc as the canonical runbook and living playbook for day-to-day capacity decisions, incident response, and safe deploys for inference services.

Quick links
- GPU fleet & capacity guide: /confluence/eng-infra/terraform-and-iac/infra-iac-and-gpu-fleet-guide-2026
- Primary runbook: /confluence/eng-infra/runbooks/gpu-capacity-and-infra-runbook-2026
- Terraform modules registry: internal-modules.redwood.local

1) Scope and goals

- Scope: All hosted and dedicated GPU pools used by Redwood inference services, plus related cloud accounts, VPCs, and IaC modules used to provision them. Includes build & CI pipelines that produce server/container images and infrastructure changes.
- Goals:
  - Maintain >=99.9% availability for inference serving clusters (see SLOs).
  - Keep 14-day runway for GPU capacity vs projected usage at 95th percentile.
  - Standardize Terraform modules and CI/CD patterns for safe rollouts and automated recovery.

2) Ownership and contacts

- Primary owner_team: engineering (infra & platform subteams)
- Team owners:
  - GPU fleet capacity & provisioning: infra-gpu-team (owner: @Priya Nambiar)
  - Cloud accounts & networking (VPCs, peering): cloud-networking-team (owner: @Marta Alvarez)
  - Terraform modules & registry: infra-iac-team (owner: @Liam O'Connor)
  - CI/CD pipelines & build images: platform-ci-team (owner: @Kai Matsuda)
- Pager escalation: see runbook page for oncall roster (links: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks)

3) Key definitions and SLOs

- Warm GPU pool: reserved instances available for burst and predictable routing. Warm pools target <5s cold-start for new sessions.
- Capacity runway: number of days before we must add capacity to meet 95th percentile traffic. Target: >=14 days.
- Inference cluster SLOs: availability 99.9% per region, p50 latency <60ms (short strings), p95 latency <200ms for 2k token sequences.

4) Capacity planning process (quarterly + runway triggers)

- Quarterly planning: infra-gpu-team runs a capacity forecast 6 weeks before the next quarter. Inputs: per-route historical tail-QPS, growth multipliers from product, model change plans (new larger models), and past autoscaler behavior.
- Runway monitoring: automated job runs daily and writes to capacity-dashboard. Triggers:
  1. Green: runway >= 30 days -> no action.
  2. Amber: runway 14-30 days -> create a capacity request and schedule procurement/reserve.
  3. Red: runway <14 days -> open a high-priority capacity ticket, notify oncall, and start emergency provisioning workflow.
- Emergency provisioning workflow (if Red):
  1. Validate forecast inputs and recent traffic spikes.
  2. Check spare capacity in other regions / dedicated pools.
  3. If cross-region capacity available, initiate smart routing fallback for non-sensitive workloads (per routing policy).
  4. If procurement needed, request reserved capacity (cloud or bare-metal partner) using the procurement playbook.
  5. As a last resort, enable aggressive eviction/reduction policies on non-critical batch jobs and temporarily reduce per-request max tokens for low-tier customers.

5) GPU types, allocation strategy, and tagging

- Preferred types: H100 (latency-sensitive production), A100 (cost-effective for mid-latency), T4/GPU-accelerator for non-critical batch/embeddings.
- Allocation policy: small models -> shared pools (A100), large models/low-latency -> H100 dedicated nodes.
- Required tags on every GPU node: environment:<prod|staging|dev>, region:<region>, gpu-type:<H100|A100|T4>, owner_team:<team>, cost-center:<id>.
- Example Terraform tag block:
  tags = ["environment:prod", "region:us-west-2", "gpu-type:H100", "owner_team:infra-gpu"]

6) Cloud accounts and networking standards

- Account structure:
  - prod-root (shared infra services)
  - prod-gpu-<region> (GPU fleets)
  - sandbox-gpu
  - staging
- VPCs: each GPU fleet resides in a regional VPC with dedicated subnet ranges for compute, storage, and management. Use /20 CIDRs for GPU compute subnets by default.
- Peering & routing: prefer VPC Peering for low-latency regional communication; use Transit Gateway when cross-region mesh needed. Ensure peering connections are documented in the networking registry.
- Security groups & firewall rules:
  - Inference nodes accept inbound on 443 from the load-balancer subnets and on SSH from bastion hosts only.
  - Control plane ports (metrics, tracing) restricted to trusted monitoring subnets.
- IP allocation: Reserve at least 10% headroom in IP assignment for autoscaling.

7) Terraform/IaC module conventions

- Modules naming: redwood-<purpose>-<resource>. Examples: redwood-gpu-pool-ec2, redwood-vpc-core, redwood-iam-gpu-service.
- Module versioning: SemVer tags required. Modules must include CHANGELOG.md and a migration doc for breaking changes.
- Registry policy: publish vetted modules to internal-modules.redwood.local. Only modules with a signed review from infra-iac-team can be used in prod.
- State management: remote state in S3 (encrypted) + DynamoDB locking for AWS accounts. Use unique state prefixes: redwood/<account>/<region>/<env>.
- Example PR checklist for infra changes:
  1. Terraform validate & plan produced and uploaded to PR.
  2. Plan approved by at least one infra-iac reviewer.
  3. Canary apply in staging, smoke tests green.
  4. Apply to prod via pipeline with manual approval.

8) CI/CD & build pipeline guidance

- Repos: infrastructure-as-code repos are colocated under github.com/redwood-infra/.
- Pipeline engine: GitHub Actions + self-hosted runners in a secure management account.
- Build images: Build container images in central repo 'redwood/base-images' tagged by build-id and base-OS. Keep reproducible builds and pinned package versions.
- Deploy stages:
  1. PR validations: lint, fmt, terraform init & validate, terragrunt / cdktf checks where applicable.
  2. Plan job: generates plan and stores artifact.
  3. Staging apply: automatic for infra changes with no prod impact; otherwise manual.
  4. Prod apply: manual approval, run by designated approver role.
- Rollback strategy: keep previous Terraform state snapshots and container images; to rollback a service, redeploy previous image tag and run a reverse-apply for Terraform if the change is infra-related.

9) Runbooks & incident playbooks (GPU capacity outage example)

- Symptoms:
  - Autoscaler failing to scale up new pods due to insufficient nodes.
  - Queues/backlogs in inference routers increasing beyond thresholds.
  - Elevated p95/p99 latency and request errors with 429 or 503.

- Immediate actions (first 15 minutes):
  1. Acknowledge pager and assemble incident lead + infra engineer.
  2. Check capacity dashboard and recent scale events.
  3. Run diagnostic commands:
     - kubectl get nodes -o wide --selector=gpu-pool=<pool-name>
     - kubectl describe node <node-name>
     - aws ec2 describe-instances --filters "Name=tag:gpu-type,Values=H100" --region us-west-2
     - check autoscaler logs in /logs/autoscaler/<cluster>/latest
  4. If nodes are provisioning but not joining, inspect cloud-init logs and kubelet service on the instance.

- Remediation steps (15-60 minutes):
  1. If OOM or kubelet crash: cordon and drain affected nodes, scale replacement nodes.
  2. If cloud provider quota reached: request quota bump via cloud-accounts runbook or failover to other regions.
  3. If provisioning errors in Terraform module: revert the last IaC change and reapply the last known-good plan.
  4. If permanent shortage: enable emergency routing to dedicated pools or scale down low-priority jobs.

- Post incident: write postmortem in /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/postmortems, include timelines, root cause, mitigation, and action items with owners and deadlines.

10) Common troubleshooting commands and telemetry

- Kubernetes: kubectl get pods -n inference, kubectl logs -f deployment/inference-router, kubectl top nodes
- Cloud: aws ec2 describe-instances --filters, aws service-quotas get-service-quota --service-code ec2 --quota-code L-0263D0A3 (example)
- Metrics to check: GPU utilization, GPU memory pressure, node launch latency, autoscaler scale-time, queue depth, p95/p99 latency.
- Dashboards: gpu-capacity-dashboard, autoscaler-health, inference-latency-traces (links in monitoring registry).

11) Change and release checklist (for infra impacting GPU pools)

- Pre-merge:
  - Terraform fmt & validate pass.
  - Plan uploaded with clear diff and owner notes.
  - Tests: staging smoke, canary load-test, integration with routing.
- Pre-rollout:
  - Notify slack channel #infra-deploy and relevant owners.
  - Schedule maintenance window if expected risk > medium.
- Post-rollout:
  - Monitor capacity & latency for 60 minutes.
  - Revert if metrics breach thresholds.

12) Known limitations and ongoing initiatives

- Known: cross-region routing occasionally adds 20-50ms tail latency; we are piloting Transit Gateway optimizations.
- Initiative: automated capacity bidding in spot markets to reduce cost for batch workloads (target Q3 2026).

13) Appendices

- Useful links and artifacts:
  - Terraform module registry: internal-modules.redwood.local
  - Capacity dashboard: dashboards.redwood.internal/gpu-capacity
  - Procurement playbook: /confluence/finance-and-legal/procurement/gpu-hardware-procurement
  - Oncall roster & runbooks: /confluence/oncall-and-incident-response/runbooks

If you are unsure about an action during an incident, escalate to the oncall infra lead. Update this page after any significant change; include test results and migration notes when updating IaC modules.
